entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15778"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Acts.10.1-Acts.10.48">Ac 10:1-48</reference>. Accession and Baptism of Cornelius and His Party; or, The First-fruits of the Gentiles.</title> <div sID="gen30395" type="x-p"/> We here enter on an entirely new phase of the Christian Church, the "opening of the door of faith to the Gentiles"; in other words, the recognition of Gentile, on terms of perfect equality with Jewish, discipleship without the necessity of circumcision. Some beginnings appear to have been already made in this direction (see on <reference osisRef="Acts.11.20">Ac 11:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.11.21">21</reference>); and Saul probably acted on this principle from the first, both in Arabia and in Syria and Cilicia. But had he been the prime mover in the admission of uncircumcised Gentiles into the Church, the Jewish party, who were never friendly to him, would have acquired such strength as to bring the Church to the verge of a disastrous schism. But on Peter, "the apostle" specially "of the circumcision," was conferred the honor of initiating this great movement, as before of the first admission of Jewish believers. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.16.19">Mt 16:19</reference>). After this, however, one who had already come upon the stage was to eclipse this "chiefest of the apostles."<div eID="gen30395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30396" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15778"/><hi type="bold">1-2. An ancient coin makes express mention of such a cohort in Syria. [Akerman, Numismatic Illustrations of the New Testament.] <div eID="gen30397" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15783"/><div sID="gen30407" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15783"/><hi type="bold">7-8. when the angel ... was departed, he called--</hi>immediately doing as directed, and thereby showing the simplicity of his faith.<div eID="gen30407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30408" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a devout soldier of them that waited on him continually--</hi>of the "soldiers under him," such as the centurion at Capernaum had (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.9">Mt 8:9</reference>). Who this "devout soldier" was, can only be matter of conjecture. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15790"/><div sID="gen30417" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15790"/><hi type="bold">17-24. while Peter doubted ... what this should mean, behold, the three men ... stood before the gate ... and asked--</hi>"were inquiring," that is, in the act of doing so. The preparations here made--of Peter for his Gentile visitors, as of Cornelius for him--are devoutly to be noted. But besides this, at the same moment, "the Spirit" expressly informs him that three men were inquiring for him, and bids him unhesitatingly go with them, as sent by Him. <div eID="gen30417" type="x-p"/>
